festivals.about: The Tulu New Year. Early in the morning the family first sees the 'Bisu kani' – rice, fruits, vegetables, gold and a lamp arranged before the deity.
Marks the end of the season of festivals, jatres and Yakshagana before the monsoon and the start of paddy farming.
In the rainy month of Aati people drink 'paale kashaya', a bitter drink from the bark of the paale tree, believed to protect health.
A folk performer dressed in leaves and a tall hat visits homes in Aati, singing and dancing to drive away illness and misfortune.
Pairs of buffaloes race through slushy paddy fields guided by a runner – a celebrated rural sport of Tulunadu.

festivals.when: Through the year, mostly in winter
festivals.about: Ritual worship of local spirit deities (daivas) such as Panjurli and Guliga, with paddanas (oral epics), costumes and dance.
An all-night dance-drama with music, songs, bright costumes and crowns, telling stories from the epics and Tulu legends.
Worship of the snake deity at sacred groves (naagabana), with offerings of milk and flowers.
Dancers painted as tigers perform to the beat of drums in the streets.
A three-day festival honouring Mother Earth; farm work rests, and special food is prepared.
